name: headless-component
intent: Publish a widget's behaviour - state, event handling, keyboard and ARIA wiring - as a headless primitive that the consumer renders with its own markup, so one interaction implementation serves many visual designs instead of being forked or restyled around.
problem: A widget's behaviour is worth reusing, but it ships tangled with one component's markup: consumers that need a different element structure, different class names or a different styling solution must copy the logic or bend their design around the shipped DOM, and every copy re-implements the keyboard, focus and ARIA behaviour. The recurring decision is how an interaction primitive hands its state and event wiring to an unknown call site without dictating what that call site renders.
context: Component-based UI codebases - web (React, Vue, Angular) and native (Compose, SwiftUI, Blazor, WPF, Qt, Swing/JavaFX) - where a design system or widget library must ship one interaction (combobox, menu, dialog, tabs, tooltip, disclosure) across several visual variants, or where an application must integrate an interaction into markup it already owns. It applies where the reuse mechanism can carry a caller-supplied render value: hooks, render props, scoped slots, slot APIs, content templates or headless directives. It does not apply when the look is the product, when a single call site owns both halves, or when the platform control already has the semantics the consumer wants.
benefits: One behaviour, many designs: the same interaction logic serves every visual variant - element structure, class names and styling solution stay the consumer's choice - so themes and brands do not fork the logic.

The interaction is implemented and tested once: keyboard handling, focus management, generated ids and ARIA attributes live in the primitive, and every new consumer inherits them instead of re-deriving them.
The behaviour is testable without a renderer: state and prop getters are plain data and functions, so transitions can be exercised in isolation rather than through mounted UI or DOM snapshots.
Clean integration: the consumer adds no wrapper element and no enforced markup, so existing CSS, form semantics and layout survive untouched.
Composable primitives: headless pieces stack (a menu primitive inside a dialog primitive; one state machine behind several framework adapters) because neither owns the other's DOM.
Incremental adoption: a component library can extract the behaviour first and re-skin later, and a consumer can restyle a single part without replacing the whole widget.
tradeoffs: The call site is bigger and more explicit: the consumer renders every part and spreads every prop getter, so a plain styled component would be shorter wherever one design is enough.

The published surface is a public contract to version: state shape, getters, handler composition, ref merging and controlled/uncontrolled props become API, and a missed or mis-ordered spread breaks behaviour silently at runtime instead of failing to compile.

Accessibility stops being automatic: because the consumer owns the DOM, correct roles, aria-* wiring and focus order depend on both sides of the contract, so a mis-applied primitive reproduces exactly the accessibility bugs it was meant to remove.
Assembly cost: unstyled primitives ship no look at all, so each design system must build the visuals and the examples that show which getter belongs on which element.

Mechanism coupling: a primitive written as a hook, a render prop, a slot or a directive usually does not port to another framework, and the indirection is pure overhead where one component could own both halves.
Escape hatches leak: controlled state, imperative handles and refs add API surface that must be documented and versioned, and every seam is a compatibility liability.

participants.responsibility: Owns the widget's state and transitions plus the keyboard, focus and ARIA policy; publishes state and prop getters (or actions) and renders no markup of its own.
Returns the attributes, ids, refs and event handlers a consumer must spread onto the corresponding element, composing consumer-supplied handlers and refs instead of overwriting them.
Supplies the element structure, styling and content, spreads each getter on the right element and renders from the published state - it carries the markup half of the contract.
The explicit states and transitions behind the behaviour (expanded, selected, active index, validation); making them explicit is what keeps the primitive predictable and testable.

Re-runs the consumer's rendering when the primitive's state changes (React re-render, Vue reactivity, Compose recomposition, SwiftUI diffing, Blazor render, delegate repaint) - without it the split has no live behaviour.

use_cases: Design systems shipping one interaction (combobox, select, menu, dialog, tabs, tooltip, disclosure) in several visual variants for different brands, densities or element structures.
A component library that must work with the consumer's styling solution and DOM instead of shipping its own wrapper elements and class names.

Application code that needs the same interaction behaviour in unrelated places - a typeahead, a focus trap, roving keyboard navigation, outside-click dismissal - without adopting the library's visuals.
Data-heavy widgets (tables, trees, command palettes) whose rows, cells and items must be rendered by the consuming application from its own data types.
Porting an interaction to another framework: one framework-agnostic state machine with per-framework adapters keeps the behaviour identical while the markup changes.
Testing interaction logic in isolation: state and getter contracts exercised without mounting a UI, leaving integration to the consumers' own tests.

Cross-framework component libraries: one framework-agnostic state machine (xstate or equivalent) with per-framework headless adapters keeps the behaviour bit-identical across React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, and native platforms, eliminating the need to re-implement interaction logic for each ecosystem.

RTL (right-to-left) and internationalisation testing: because the accessibility contract lives in the primitive, testing keyboard interaction, focus order, and ARIA semantics in an RTL layout is isolated from visual styling, making it practical to validate in CI.

Multi-brand and white-label design systems: the same headless primitives (tabs, combobox, dialog) serve multiple brands that each bring their own design tokens, class names and element structures, avoiding the fork of behaviour per brand that a styled-component approach would require.

CMS-driven content sites: headless CMS content (Sanity, Contentful) rendered into headless primitives (Disclosure, Accordion, Tabs) where the CMS supplies the panel content and the site supplies the visual design — the CMS never touches markup or styles, only structured content.

Design token integration: a brand system with token-driven spacing, colour, and typography passes those tokens to headless primitives via a Theme context; the primitives consume tokens but emit no styles, so the same behaviour works across light/dark/high-contrast themes without any code change.

Animation library integration: headless primitives emit state changes (open/close, activeIndex) that animation libraries (Framer Motion, Motion One) consume to drive transitions; the primitive remains the single source of truth for interaction state while the animation library owns the visual transition, keeping concerns cleanly separated.

A/B testing and feature flags: a headless Dialog primitive can be composed with a feature-flag wrapper that conditionally mounts either a rich visual variant or a minimal fallback, without the primitive knowing about the flag — enabling a/b testing of interaction UX independently of visual design.

Micro-frontend / module federation: shared headless primitives (published as a federated module) provide interaction consistency across independently-deployed micro-frontends; each team brings its own visual design but the keyboard, focus, and ARIA behaviour is guaranteed identical across all federated pieces.

Storybook-driven documentation: ship headless primitives with stories that demonstrate every getter applied to the right element, using Storybook's Controls and Actions addons to let documentation readers exercise every state transition and inspect the getter output — turning the accessibility contract into an interactive reference rather than a static doc.

White-label product lines: a SaaS product serving multiple vertical markets (healthcare, finance, retail) uses the same headless primitive set with per-vertical Tailwind config overrides; each market gets a visually distinct product that behaves identically at the interaction level, and regulatory accessibility testing covers all markets simultaneously.

Cross-framework product lines: Ark UI ships the same headless components (dialog, tabs, select, date picker) with an identical API for React, Vue, Solid and Svelte because a shared Zag.js finite state machine drives every adapter - the interaction is written once and behaves identically across ecosystems while each app supplies its own markup.

Adobe React Spectrum: React Aria hooks return the accessibility props (roles, aria-* attributes, event handlers) for buttons, dialogs, listboxes and pickers, and the application - or the React Aria Components layer on top - supplies the markup, so the behaviour is audited once against the ARIA contract and reused across the product family.

shadcn/ui distribution: applications copy Radix headless primitives together with their Tailwind markup into their own repository, so the composition of each primitive becomes consumer-owned source - a distribution form of the pattern in which the headless behaviour stays a dependency while the markup half is edited in place.
avoid_when: The visual design is the product (chart, icon set, illustration, animation): ship a styled component instead of a behaviour with no look.
A single call site owns both behaviour and markup: a local component or plain state is simpler, because the split only pays off with multiple consumers.
The team cannot maintain a public contract: getters, state shape and escape hatches need documentation, types and tests, or consumers will misuse them.
The platform control already carries the semantics you need (input, select, details/summary, dialog): style or extend the native control instead of rebuilding its behaviour.
The behaviour is small enough that a styled component with two props covers it: a prop-getter contract is more machinery than the widget deserves.
anti_patterns: Headless in name only: the primitive still renders wrapper elements and depends on its own class names, so consumers must strip styles to use it.
Getters that overwrite the consumer's props instead of composing them: spreading a getter after the consumer's onClick silently discards the consumer's handler.
Exposing internal state as a mutable object the consumer writes directly, so the primitive can no longer enforce its own transitions or invariants.
Forking the behaviour per visual variant (one styled component per design), which is exactly the duplication the headless split exists to remove.

Shipping the primitive without an accessibility contract or tests: because the consumer owns the DOM, an unverified contract breaks silently and surfaces as broken keyboard or screen-reader behaviour.

Prop getter with too many arguments: if getButtonProps(options) requires more than two or three options, the primitive is leaking UI assumptions into its API and will fracture when a new visual variant needs a different element.

Silent state divergence: the primitive has a tested behaviour and the consumer has tested markup, but their composition is never tested together, so the accessibility contract is validated only in isolation and breaks silently in integration.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: behaviour and presentation are different responsibilities with different owners.
Information hiding / encapsulation: the primitive publishes only the state and operations the markup needs, and keeps its internals private.
Open/closed principle: new visual designs arrive as consumers, not as edits to the primitive.
Single source of truth: one owner of the widget state, from which the rendered markup derives rather than duplicating it.
Composition over inheritance: behaviour is composed into the consumer's tree instead of being inherited from a widget base class.
Least knowledge: the consumer knows only the published getters and state, never the primitive's internal structure.

Invariant enforcement: illegal state transitions must be impossible in the primitive — if a tab cannot be selected before its panel is mounted, the primitive enforces that constraint, not the consumer.

Explicit over implicit: keyboard interactions, focus targets, and ARIA derivations are traceable to an explicit state and a documented APG mapping, not to scattered if/else branches that are hard to audit.

Consumer auditability: because the consumer owns the rendered DOM, every aria attribute must be derivable from the primitive's state machine output, so an accessibility auditor can trace any screen-reader behaviour back to the primitive's contract and not to ad-hoc markup.
best_practices: Publish getters (functions) rather than pre-built prop objects, so ids, aria-* state and handlers stay consistent and the consumer can merge its own props and refs.
Compose event handlers (call every handler in order) and merge refs instead of replacing them, and document the merge semantics.
Keep the state machine explicit and deterministic, derive every aria attribute from it, and make illegal transitions impossible or loud.
Fail loudly on misuse: a getter called for the wrong element, a missing required context, or a part used outside the primitive should raise a diagnostic instead of rendering nothing.
Keep the behaviour core framework-free where the ecosystem allows it (a pure state machine plus per-framework adapters), so the same logic can serve several frameworks.
Test the accessibility contract (roles, aria wiring, keyboard interaction, focus order) and ship an example per supported styling approach - unstyled primitives are unusable without assembly docs.
Version the public surface (state shape, getters, controlled/uncontrolled props) and treat it as an API from the first release.

Support both controlled and uncontrolled APIs simultaneously, mirroring native HTML input behaviour: expose value + onChange (controlled) alongside defaultValue/defaultChecked (uncontrolled); never force a single mode, as design-system consumers need both for internal state vs form-integration use cases.

Define and publish the accessibility contract as a first-class artifact — roles, aria-attribute derivations, keyboard interactions, and focus management must be documented in terms of the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide patterns the primitive implements, not just implied by the getter output.

Handle portal rendering explicitly for dialogs, tooltips and popovers: when the primitive renders into a portal (document.body, a floating layer), the focus trap, aria-modal, and aria-labelledby ids must follow the portal DOM location, and the primitive must expose a mechanism for the consumer to wire the portal correctly.

Design a TypeScript-first API: prop getter return types, state shape, and event handler signatures are the public contract; consumers in typed languages will hit runtime errors without compile-time safety, so publish discriminated-union state types andBranded prop-getter return types that guide correct usage.

Align the state machine with the W3C ARIA APG keyboard contract for the target pattern (roving tabindex for listbox/combobox/menu; aria-activedescendant for combobox; sequential focus navigation for dialog); choosing the wrong focus strategy is the most common accessibility regression in headless components.

Expose a useHeadless<T> adapter pattern for framework integration: a generic useHeadless(behavior, frameworkAdapter) hook that takes a pure state-machine behaviour and a lightweight framework adapter (React/Vue/Angular/Compose/SwiftUI), keeping the core logic portable while each framework gets its idiomatic reactive primitive.

For portal-rendered primitives (Dialog, Tooltip, Popover): the focus trap, aria-modal, and aria-labelledby/idrefs must travel with the portal DOM node; expose a named slot or render-prop for the portal root so the consumer can wire accessibility ids correctly after the portal mounts — not before.

Publish the behaviour core as a separate entry-point from the framework adapter (e.g. headless-core.js vs headless-react.js): consumers who only need the state machine for testing or server-side logic should not pull in the React/Vue runtime, keeping initial bundle impact proportional to what is actually used.

Freeze the prop-getter return shape with a branded type (TypeScript): using a nominal/b branded type for the getter return (e.g. `ButtonProps & {__brand: 'ButtonProps'}`) prevents consumers from spreading the raw object onto the wrong element type and makes the 'wrong element' failure a compile-time error rather than a runtime accessibility bug.

Decouple the state machine from the reactivity layer: define the machine as a pure function (state × event → state) with no side effects, and keep all framework reactivity (useState, watch, observe) in a thin adapter; this makes the machine testable with a simple table-driven test without any framework mounted.

For controlled/uncontrolled coexistence: implement the 'read-both-write-one' pattern — the getter always reads both the controlled value (prop) and the internal state, and the write path (onChange) always writes through to the consumer's handler; never attempt to 'merge' controlled and uncontrolled into one state — they are mutually exclusive ownership models.

Run axe-core against every rendered example in CI: because the consumer owns the markup, a headless primitive with no shipped visuals cannot catch accessibility regressions without a rendered example; ship at least one composed example per supported styling approach (CSS classes, Tailwind, CSS-in-JS) and run axe on each in CI.

Model state as a discriminated union (TypeScript) rather than a flat object: `type DisclosureState = { status: 'closed' } | { status: 'open' }` — discriminated unions make illegal state combinations unrepresentable at the type level and make exhaustive switch completion checking a compile-time guarantee, not a runtime convention.

Document which ARIA attributes the primitive manages and which the consumer must NOT override: publish a 'managed attributes' list alongside the getter API; attributes in this list are set by the primitive and overriding them (even with a different value) is a contract violation, not a customization point.

Kent C. Dodds, 'How to give rendering control to users with prop getters' (October 2017): prop getters as the mechanism that lets a component hand rendering to the consumers of the component, and the article that introduced downshift, 'the first library to implement this pattern'.
https://kentcdodds.com/blog/how-to-give-rendering-control-to-users-with-prop-getters
https://www.downshift-js.com/
https://headlessui.com/
https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/introduction
https://zagjs.com/overview/introduction

Martin Fowler, 'Headless Component: a pattern for composing React UIs': formalises the pattern with a custom-hook delivery mechanism, emphasises DRY separation of behaviour from presentation and multiple visual representations from the same logic. https://martinfowler.com/articles/headless-component.html

Merrick Christensen, 'Headless User Interface Components': frames headless as a 'bring your own interface' pattern, cites Downshift (Kent C. Dodds) as the canonical real-world exemplar. https://mercoderchristensen.com/articles/headless-user-interface-components

React RFC #58 — 'React.HeadlessComponent': formal RFC proposing a first-class React.HeadlessComponent base type to give tooling visibility (devtools distinction) and enable renderless composition. https://github.com/reactjs/rfcs/pull/58

W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) — Patterns: the canonical reference for all ARIA contracts (Dialog, Listbox, Combobox, Tabs, Treeview, etc.), specifying required roles, aria-* attributes, keyboard interactions, and focus management strategy (roving tabindex vs aria-activedescendant). https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/

chromvoid/headless-ui ADR-001 — headless architecture: a11y contracts defined as first-class public API shaped around createX / get*Props / actions/selectors; modules layered: core → interactions → a11y-contracts → adapters. https://github.com/chromvoid/headless-ui/blob/main/specs/ADR-001-headless-architecture.md

chromvoid/headless-ui ADR-004 — focus-selection policy: defines roving-tabindex vs aria-activedescendant strategy selection, focus invariants (activeId must be valid option or null), baseline keyboard contract (Arrow keys, Home/End, Space, Enter, Escape), and APG props contract. https://github.com/chromvoid/headless-ui/blob/main/specs/ADR-004-focus-selection-policy.md

David Khourshid, 'Infinitely Better UIs with Finite Automata' (slides): FSM pattern for UIs — define machine (state → action → next state + optional side-effect command); local per-component machines with actor-model communication; contrasts with Redux's global store. https://slides.com/davidkpiano/finite-state-machines

Full Stack Radio EP 130 — 'Building Better UI Components with State Machines' with David Khourshid: boolean flags cause bugs; xstate returns a single state object (value + context) rather than many scattered flags; enables automatic test generation from state machine descriptions. https://www.fullstackradio.com/130

Nazar Boyko, 'Headless UI Components: Flexibility With Responsibility': covers pitfalls including over-abstraction, prop-getter complexity, accessibility neglect, and focus/ARIA misuse. https://www.nazarboyko.com/articles/headless-ui-components-flexibility-with-responsibility

Conrad Koh, 'shadcn-base-ui-migration' guide: incremental migration strategy from Radix UI to Base UI — atomic-first migration order, breaking-change mapping (asChild→render, data-[state=*]→data-open/data-closed, onSelect→onClick). https://github.com/conradkoh/chatroom/blob/master/docs/developer/shadcn-base-ui-migration.md

React Aria (Adobe): hook-based headless components returning prop handlers for accessibility — the props-to-elements model that React Aria Components (RAC) builds on. https://react-spectrum.adobe.com/react-aria/

React Aria Components (RAC):opinionated headless components built on React Aria hooks, shipping both behaviour and default markup, targeting teams that want a complete accessible baseline to restyle. https://react.dev/reference/react-aria

Zag.js — Finite state machine powered headless component patterns for React, Solid, Vue and Angular; each machine is framework-agnostic and adapters translate to framework-specific primitives. https://zagjs.com/overview/introduction

LogRocket blog: 'How to make your design system DRY with Zag' — explains state-machine-first approach where each component state is modelled as a machine (open/closed, activeIndex), keeping behaviour testable in isolation. https://blog.logrocket.com

shadcn/ui architecture: copy-paste distribution of Radix UI headless primitives colocated with Tailwind markup; the 'ownership' model (code lives in consumer's repo, not node_modules) is a distribution variant that makes headless primitives zero-dependency and fully customisable. https://ui.shadcn.com/docs

Matt Wong, 'shadcn/ui Architecture: Own Your Components, Not a Dependency' — analyses the copy-paste distribution model and how it combines Radix headless primitives with consumer-owned styling. https://www.matthewswong.com/en/blog/shadcn-ui-component-architecture

Martin Fowler, 'Headless Component' (updated November 2023): the canonical software-pattern writeup; introduces the hook-based delivery (useDisclosure, useListbox), emphasises that the pattern's value multiplies with the number of visual variants and that the behaviour/testing isolation is the primary win. https://martinfowler.com/articles/headless-component.html

React RFC #58 — 'React.HeadlessComponent': proposed a first-class React.HeadlessComponent base type to give tooling devtools visibility and enable renderless composition; closed but influential on subsequent library design. https://github.com/reactjs/rfcs/pull/58

W3C ARIA APG — Dialog pattern: covers aria-modal, aria-labelledby, focus trap, focus restoration on close, andEscape key handling; required reading for any headless dialog or modal primitive. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/

W3C ARIA APG — Listbox pattern: covers roving tabindex management, aria-activedescendant as an alternative, keyboard arrows, typeahead, and multi-select aria-checked wiring. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/listbox/
W3C ARIA APG — Tabs pattern: covers automatic vs manual activation semantics, aria-selected, and keyboard focus movement. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/
W3C ARIA APG — Menu pattern: covers menubar vs menu bar distinction, aria-haspopup, keyboard arrow navigation, and separator role. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/menu/

TKDodo, 'Building Type-Safe Compound Components' (January 2026): contrasts compound components with headless hooks; compound components use implicit context sharing while headless hooks use explicit prop getters, and the two patterns can be combined (headless state machine + compound component API surface). https://tkdodo.eu

Sandro Roth, 'Building Component Slots in React' (November 2022): explains slot pattern — passing elements to a component that renders them in named locations — as a complement to headless: slots provide the markup locations, headless provides the behaviour wiring. https://sandroroth.com

Someantics.dev, 'Accessible Components with State Machines and Zag' (July 2022): explains how Zag decomposes each widget into a set of finite states captured in a readable, shareable state machine, separating the logic from any framework rendering. https://someantics.dev

David Khourshid (Microsoft), 'Infinitely Better UIs with Finite Automata' (GitHub slides): FSM pattern for UIs — define machine (state → action → next state + optional side-effect command); local per-component machines with actor-model communication; contrasts with Redux's global store. https://slides.com/davidkpiano/finite-state-machines

React RFC #163 — 'React Hooks': the foundational mechanism behind modern headless delivery; useState/useReducer/useCallback/useRef are the primitives from which headless hooks are composed. https://github.com/reactjs/rfcs/blob/main/text/0067-react-hook-element.md

downshift-js: the canonical real-world exemplar of the prop-getter pattern; useCombobox and useSelect hooks ship with Downshift and have been production-tested at scale since 2017. https://www.downshift-js.com/

Andrico's blog, 'Defining your UI library's testing strategy' (August 2021): 3-tier strategy (unit/integration/snapshot) applied to headless component libraries; argues headless primitives are the most unit-testable layer because behaviour is framework-independent. https://blog.andri.co

Deque Systems, 'Writing Automated Tests for Accessibility' (January 2018): axe-core integration strategies for headless components; because the primitive owns ARIA wiring, accessibility tests can be run against prop-getter output without mounting. https://www.deque.com

Tailwind Labs / Headless UI GitHub issue #666: Portal rendering issue — when Headless UI Dialog renders into a portal (document.body), shadow-DOM styles from the host web component do not apply; demonstrates the portal-crossing seam issue. https://github.com

Chromvoid headless-ui ADR-001 and ADR-004: canonical a11y contract and focus-selection policy documentation; ADR-001 defines layered architecture (core → interactions → a11y-contracts → adapters) and ADR-004 defines roving-tabindex vs aria-activedescendant selection with baseline keyboard contract. https://github.com/chromvoid/headless-ui

Semantic Versioning for UI component libraries: headless primitives are API-stable once state shape and getter signatures are published; any new required prop or removed getter is a breaking change regardless of semver label, making a public changelog as important as the semver string.

Kelly Mears, 'Headless Component' (design note): a headless primitive provides behaviour and accessibility - keyboard handling, focus, ARIA, positioning, scroll locking - with the consumer supplying the look; API shape (value types, committed vs continuous events) and portalling are the design decisions to get right. https://kellymears.me/knowledge/design/headless-component

Ark UI (chakra-ui/ark): unstyled, accessible components driven by Zag.js finite state machines with an identical API across React, Solid, Vue and Svelte - a production cross-framework headless set. https://github.com/chakra-ui/ark
Base UI: unstyled accessible React components built to W3C ARIA practices and WCAG 2.2, positioned as the base layer for custom design systems. https://base-ui.com/

Graham The Dev, 'Headless-UI "Fully Accessible" - it's not your fault you believe the BS': criticism of ARIA-first headless components - a wrong semantic base patched with ARIA degrades rather than improves accessibility, and the abstraction adds bundle weight and maintenance cost. https://dev.to/grahamthedev/headless-ui-fully-accessible-it-s-not-your-fault-you-believe-the-bs-accessibility-rants-582j

shadcn-ui/ui issue #11724, 'Bundle size audit of a minimal admin panel across base / aria / radix (measured, reproducible)': identical 12-component app measured across three headless bases shows the behaviour cores differ by tens of kB gzipped (React Aria base ~42 kB heavier than Radix) - evidence that headless behaviour has a real payload cost. https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui/issues/11724
